message.content:
Write a self-contained HTML drill/quiz file to this exact path:
/home/node/work/normal_work/HFT_Trading_Practice_Repo/docs/learning/drills/0004-itch-order-book-latency.html

Use the dark-theme style (same CSS variables: --bg:#0f1117, --surface:#1a1d27, --surface2:#22263a, --border:#2e3450, --accent:#5b8dee, --accent2:#a78bfa, --green:#34d399, --yellow:#fbbf24, --red:#f87171, --text:#e2e8f0, --muted:#94a3b8, --code-bg:#0d1117). Inline all CSS. max-width 820px container.

Title: "Drill 0004 — ITCH 5.0 Order Book Reconstruction and Latency"

Include a scoreboard at the top showing: score, total questions, accuracy %, and a progress bar. Update them dynamically via JS.

Include 8 multiple-choice questions (MCQ) and 3 written-recall questions.

=== MCQ QUESTIONS ===

Q1: What does the 2-byte length prefix in the MoldUDP64 framing represent?
A) The message sequence number
B) The number of bytes in the following message payload (correct)
C) The stock locate code
D) The ITCH protocol version

Q2: In ITCH 5.0, the price field for an Add Order message contains 1502500. What is the real price in dollars?
A) $1,502,500
B) $1502.50
C) $150.25 (correct)
D) $15.0250

Q3: Which C++ data structure stores per-price bid levels in the baseline OrderBook and ensures best_bid() is always the first element?
A) std::unordered_map with a max-heap
B) std::map<uint32_t, uint32_t, std::greater<uint32_t>> (correct)
C) std::map<uint32_t, uint32_t> (ascending)
D) std::priority_queue<uint32_t>

Q4: What happens to the orders_ hash map when an Execute Order message reduces a position to zero shares?
A) The entry remains with shares=0
B) The entry is deleted from orders_ (correct — execute() removes the entry when shares drop to zero)
C) The entry is moved to a separate 'filled_orders' map
D) Nothing — execute() only updates the price level map, not orders_

Q5: In bench_main.cpp, what does the t0–t1 window in the on_add lambda measure?
A) Time from UDP packet arrival to book update (full tick-to-trade)
B) Time from book.add() + make_signal() — the book-update-and-signal latency (correct)
C) Time spent parsing the binary message from the buffer
D) Time for the NIC to deliver the frame to the application

Q6: Why does the benchmark use CLOCK_MONOTONIC instead of CLOCK_REALTIME?
A) CLOCK_MONOTONIC has higher resolution than CLOCK_REALTIME
B) CLOCK_REALTIME can jump backward due to NTP; CLOCK_MONOTONIC never goes backward (correct)
C) CLOCK_MONOTONIC is available on all platforms; CLOCK_REALTIME is Linux-only
D) CLOCK_REALTIME has a 1-millisecond granularity on modern kernels

Q7: If the p99 latency is 420 ns and the p99.9 latency is 8200 ns, what does this tell you?
A) 99% of messages take at least 420 ns
B) 1 in 100 messages is slower than the median but faster than 420 ns
C) 999 in 1000 messages complete in under 420 ns, but 1 in 1000 spikes to ~8200 ns (correct)
D) The mean latency is between 420 ns and 8200 ns

Q8: The ReplaceOrder message contains both old_order_ref and new_order_ref. Why does it issue a new reference number instead of modifying the old one?
A) It is a Nasdaq protocol quirk; the old ref is reused internally by the exchange
B) The replace is atomic: the new order gets a new position in the queue; reusing the old ref would imply queue priority continuity (correct)
C) The parser cannot distinguish Replace from Delete without two different refs
D) The new ref is always the old ref incremented by 1

=== WRITTEN RECALL QUESTIONS ===

WR1: "Describe the full sequence of data structure operations that happen when a Replace Order message arrives at the OrderBook. Name the maps involved."

Model answer: "A Replace Order carries old_order_ref, new_order_ref, shares, and price. The OrderBook first looks up old_order_ref in orders_ (the unordered_map) to retrieve its side and price_raw, then removes its shares from the appropriate level map (bids_ or asks_). It then removes the old_order_ref entry from orders_. Next it inserts the new order into orders_ under new_order_ref with the new price and shares, and adds those shares to the correct level map."

WR2: "Explain why std::unordered_map is used for orders_ but std::map is used for bids_ and asks_. What operation requires each container?"

Model answer: "orders_ must support O(1) lookup by order_ref — given any Execute/Delete/Replace message we need to instantly find the side, price, and share count for that specific order. A hash map provides amortized O(1) lookup. bids_ and asks_ must provide the best price instantly as an iterator to the first element, and they must stay sorted. std::map (a red-black tree) keeps keys sorted and gives O(1) access to begin() which is always the best bid (highest, because std::greater comparator) or best ask (lowest, default ascending). Per-level updates are O(log n) which is acceptable because the number of distinct price levels is small."

WR3: "Why is p99.9 latency more important than mean latency when evaluating a trading system? Give one source of latency that would appear at p99.9 but not at p50."

Model answer: "Mean latency is dominated by the common case. A strategy might appear fast on average but lose money on the rare events (p99.9) when it reacts too slowly. In HFT the rare spike is exactly when market microstructure is changing — the most valuable moment to act. Sources of p99.9 spikes include: OS scheduler preempting the thread for another process, a TLB miss or page fault on a cold code path, CPU frequency scaling stepping down between bursts, or the unordered_map triggering a rehash when load factor exceeds the threshold."

Style each MCQ as a card with radio buttons. On submit show color-coded feedback (green = correct, red = wrong + show correct answer). Show written recall with a "Reveal Answer" button that expands the model answer below the textarea. Track score (MCQs only for auto-scoring). Include a reset button at the bottom.

The file should be completely self-contained HTML with inline JS and CSS. No external dependencies. Write it now.

Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.

- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
